title: NULL Summary
summary: NULL and nullptr both represent 0 and indicate an invalid address. Always check that a pointer is not NULL before dereferencing it.
main_text: NULL and nullptr both evaluate to 0. They are used to indicate an INVALID address. Before dereferencing a pointer, check that it is NOT NULL using a conditional check: if(ptr != NULL) { /* safe to dereference */ }. Three example pointer declarations are shown: int* ptr1, char* word, and double* ptr2, each containing the value 0 when set to NULL.
notes_text: NULL checking is critical for linked list operations because the end of a linked list is marked by a NULL next pointer. Forgetting to check for NULL before dereferencing leads to segmentation faults, one of the most common errors when working with linked lists.

images.description: Three memory boxes showing pointer variables (int* ptr1, char* word, double* ptr2) each containing the value 0, illustrating that NULL pointers hold the value zero regardless of the pointer type.

title: Arrays Review
summary: Arrays provide fast O(1) access using contiguous memory and address arithmetic, but cannot grow or resize once declared on the stack or heap.
main_text: Fast access: Because arrays are contiguous in memory, we can jump straight to element i with only the start address and data type. Recall the formula: start_addr + i*data_size. If we know integer element i is at location 7304, we know where element i+1 is (at 7308, since integers are 4 bytes). Can't grow (resize): Once we declare the array (either statically on the stack or dynamically on the heap) we cannot increase its size. To add one more value when the array is full, we must allocate a new larger array, copy over all existing items, then add the new value. Example code shows declaring int data[25] and accessing data[i]. Another example shows dynamically allocating with int *ptr = new int[size] and the problem of needing more than the allocated size.
notes_text: The inability of arrays to resize is the key motivation for introducing linked lists. The copy-and-reallocate approach for growing arrays is expensive at O(n) for each resize. Linked lists solve this by allowing element-by-element allocation.

images.description: Memory layout diagram showing addresses 7300-7308 with dat[0]=103, dat[1]=104, dat[2]=170 in contiguous locations, demonstrating how array elements are stored sequentially in memory.
Diagram showing the process of growing an array: old full array of 6 elements, allocating a new array of 12 slots, and copying items over then adding the new value 21.
labels: Copy over items then add value

title: Linked Lists Overview Section Divider
summary: Section divider slide marking the beginning of the Linked Lists Overview portion of the lecture.
main_text: LINKED LISTS OVERVIEW. This section begins the core discussion of linked lists as a data structure.
notes_text: This divider separates the review material (arrays, NULL) from the new linked list content that follows.

title: Analogy - Lists
summary: Lists are a natural strategy for ordered items where you can add, remove, and reorder entries. Arrays require knowing max size ahead of time.
main_text: Natural strategy when we have a set of items that require specific ordering is to create a list. Write down what you know now. Can add more items later (usually to the end of the list). Remove (cross off) others when done with them. Can only do this with an array if you know max size of list ahead of time (which is sometimes fine). We could track the start and end (aka head and tail) but only a portion would be used at a time (wasteful!). Example shows a to-do list: 1. Do CS 103 HW, 2. Join ACM or IEEE, 3. Play Video Games, 4. Watch a movie. Items can be crossed off (completed) and new items like Exercise and Eat dinner can be added. The list can also be represented as separate cards/slots rather than a numbered sequential list.
notes_text: This analogy connects the abstract concept of a list to everyday experience. The key insight is that real-world lists grow and shrink dynamically, which motivates the need for a data structure that can do the same without pre-allocating a fixed size.

images.description: Two representations of a to-do list side by side: a numbered list on the left showing items being crossed off and added, and a card/slot representation on the right where each item occupies its own box with empty slots available for growth.

title: Linked Lists Introduction
summary: A linked list stores values in separate dynamically allocated objects, each containing a pointer to the next. Only the head pointer is needed to access the list.
main_text: A linked list stores values in separate chunks of memory (i.e. a dynamically allocated object). To know where the next one is, each one stores an explicit pointer to the next. Then, all we need to do is track where the first object is (i.e. the head pointer). We can allocate more or delete old ones as needed so we only use memory as needed, changing pointers as we go. The Item struct contains two fields: int val and Item* next. The struct definition is: struct Item { int val; Item* next; };. An example linked list is shown with head pointer at 0x148 pointing to an Item with val=3 and next=0x1c0, which points to an Item with val=9 and next=0x164, which points to an Item with val=2 and next=0x0 (NULL).
notes_text: This is the fundamental definition of a singly linked list. Each node (Item) contains data and a pointer to the next node. The last node's next pointer is NULL, marking the end of the list. Unlike arrays, linked list elements can be scattered anywhere in memory -- they are connected only through pointers.

images.description: Diagram showing the Item struct blueprint as a box with two fields (int val and Item* next), and a concrete linked list with three nodes at addresses 0x148, 0x1c0, and 0x164 connected by next pointers, with the head pointer (Item* head) storing 0x148.

title: Linked List Traversal and Modification Exercise
summary: Interactive exercise asking students to determine the order of values, how to insert at the front, and how to remove a value from a linked list.
main_text: What is the order of values in this linked list? How would you insert 6 at the front of the list? How would you remove the value 4? The diagram shows a linked list with head pointer at 0x360, pointing to an Item with val=5 at address 0x360 with next=0x240. The node at 0x240 has val=4 and next=0x3e0. The node at 0x3e0 has val=1 and next=0x200. The node at 0x200 has val=8 and next=0x0 (NULL). So the order of values following the pointers from head is: 5, 4, 1, 8.
notes_text: This exercise reinforces understanding of pointer traversal. The order is determined by following next pointers from head, not by memory addresses. To insert 6 at front: create a new node with val=6, set its next to current head (0x360), update head to point to the new node. To remove 4: find the node before it (val=5), update its next to skip over 4 (point to 0x3e0), then delete the node with val=4.

images.description: Memory diagram showing four linked list nodes scattered in memory at addresses 0x200, 0x240, 0x360, and 0x3e0 with the head pointer at 0x360, demonstrating that list order follows pointers not memory addresses.

title: Arrays vs. Linked List
summary: Arrays allow O(1) random access via address arithmetic but linked lists require sequential traversal. Linked lists trade access speed for the ability to dynamically resize.
main_text: Recall: if we have the start address of an array, we can get the i-th element quickly using: start_addr + i*data_size. Question: If we have the start (head) pointer to a linked list, can we find the i-th element quickly? No! Have to walk the linked list. Items are NOT CONTIGUOUS. Linked lists trade offs: Pro: the ability to resize (grow/shrink). Con: sacrifice speed of access when attempting to get the element at an arbitrary location. Example code shows array access with int data[25] and data[20] = 7. Memory diagram shows data starting at address 100 with contiguous elements. Linked list diagram shows head pointer at 0x148 pointing to nodes at scattered addresses 0x148, 0x1c0, 0x164 with values 3, 9, 2.
notes_text: This is the core tradeoff between arrays and linked lists. Arrays give O(1) random access because elements are stored contiguously and the address can be computed directly. Linked lists require O(n) traversal in the worst case because each node could be anywhere in memory. However, linked lists can grow and shrink without costly reallocation.

images.description: Side-by-side comparison showing an array with contiguous memory addresses (100, 104, 108...) enabling direct access, versus a linked list with nodes at scattered addresses connected by pointers requiring sequential traversal.

title: In Class Coding Exercise
summary: Directs students to an EdStem/Codio exercise for hands-on practice writing a linked list implementation.
main_text: EdStem/Codio Exercise - Writing a linked list. Students are directed to complete an in-class coding exercise to practice implementing linked list operations.
notes_text: Hands-on coding is essential for understanding linked lists. This exercise likely involves implementing basic operations like push_back, which will be explained in detail in the following slides.

title: Linked List Class Overview
summary: A linked list class uses an Item struct with val and next pointer, a List class with head pointer, and supports operations like push_back, push_front, pop_back, pop_front, and find.
main_text: Use structures/classes and pointers to make linked data structures including linked lists, trees, graphs, etc. List: Arbitrarily sized collection of values. Can add or remove any number of new values. Only REQUIRED data member: head pointer (though we can add a few other members to increase efficiency). Usually supports following set of operations: Append (push_back), Prepend (push_front), Remove back item (pop_back), Remove front item (pop_front), Find (look for particular value). The Item struct is defined as: struct Item { int val; Item* next; };. The List class is defined as: class List { public: List(); ~List(); void push_back(int v); ... private: Item* head; };. An empty list has head pointing to 0x0 (NULL). Note: Use 'struct' for objects that are purely collections of data without associated operations. Use 'class' when data does have associated functions/methods.
notes_text: This slide establishes the class-based design for a linked list. The separation of Item (struct for data) and List (class for operations) follows good object-oriented design principles. The head pointer initialized to NULL represents an empty list. The destructor ~List() is needed because dynamically allocated Items must be freed.

images.description: Diagram showing the Item struct blueprint with two fields (int val and Item* next) and an empty List object with head pointer set to 0x0 (NULL).

title: Building A Linked List (1) - Constructor Initialization
summary: The List constructor should initialize the head pointer. Students are asked to determine the correct initial value for head in an empty list.
main_text: How should we initialize our list object? The constructor List::List() sets head equal to a blank (to be filled in by students). The code shows #include<iostream>, using namespace std, and the constructor with head = _____________; (blank for students to fill). In main(), a List mylist is declared, which calls the constructor. The diagram shows the head pointer box with an empty value, representing the state after construction.
notes_text: The answer is head = NULL (or nullptr). An empty linked list has no nodes, so the head pointer should be NULL to indicate there are no items. This is the starting state before any elements are added. Always initialize pointers to NULL to avoid dangling pointer issues.

images.description: Diagram showing a List object after construction with the head pointer box containing an empty/unset value, prompting students to determine the correct initialization.

title: Building A Linked List (2) - Adding an Element
summary: When adding elements to a linked list, always handle two cases: when the list is EMPTY (head is NULL) and when the list is NON-EMPTY. Items should be allocated on the heap.
main_text: How do we add an element? Anytime we code for a linked data structure we should always account for 2 cases: When the structure is EMPTY (and thus head is NULL), and when the structure is NON-EMPTY. How should we allocate our Item? On the stack or on the heap? The push_back function checks if(head == NULL) for the empty case. In the empty case, an Item newItem is created as a local variable and head is set to &newItem. The code shows: List::List() { head = NULL; } and void List::push_back(int v) { if(head == NULL) { // list is empty -- Item newItem; head = &newItem; } else { ... } }.
notes_text: This slide introduces the critical two-case pattern for linked list operations. The stack allocation shown here (Item newItem) is intentionally problematic -- it will be corrected in the next slide. Stack-allocated items are destroyed when the function returns, leaving a dangling pointer. This sets up the lesson about heap allocation.

images.description: Diagram showing head pointer at 0x0 and a separate Item struct with val and next fields, illustrating the initial state before adding the first element to an empty list.

title: Building A Linked List (3) - Dynamic Heap Allocation
summary: ALL linked list node allocations SHOULD be dynamic allocations on the heap using new, so they persist beyond the scope of the function call.
main_text: ALL allocations SHOULD be dynamic allocations on the heap so they persist beyond the scope of the push_back call. Two side-by-side examples are shown. WRONG approach (left, marked with prohibition sign): Item myitem; myitem.val = v; myitem.next = NULL; head = &myitem; -- This allocates on the stack and the item is destroyed when push_back returns, leaving a dangling pointer. CORRECT approach (right): head = new Item; head->val = v; head->next = NULL; -- This allocates on the heap using new, so the item persists after the function returns. Both show the result of mylist.push_back(3) with head at 0x148 pointing to an Item with val=3 and next=NULL.
notes_text: This is a critical lesson. Stack-allocated variables are destroyed when their scope ends. Since push_back is a function, any local Item variables die when it returns. Using 'new' allocates on the heap, where memory persists until explicitly deleted. The arrow operator (->) is used to access members through a pointer: head->val is equivalent to (*head).val.

images.description: Side-by-side comparison of wrong (stack) and correct (heap) allocation approaches for linked list nodes, both showing head at 0x148 pointing to a node with val=3 and next=NULL, but the left approach is marked as incorrect with a prohibition sign.

title: Always Handle 2 Cases
summary: When coding linked list operations, always handle the EMPTY case (head is NULL) and the NON-EMPTY case (head is NOT NULL) separately.
main_text: Handle the EMPTY case (when head is NULL): The head pointer contains 0x0, meaning no items exist in the list. Handle the NON-EMPTY case (when head is NOT NULL): The head pointer contains a valid address (e.g., 0x148) pointing to the first item. In the non-empty example, head points to a chain of three items: at 0x148 with val=3 and next=0x1c0, at 0x1c0 with val=9 and next=0x0 (NULL), and at 0x164 with val=2 and next=0x0 (NULL). The last item shown separately with its own NULL next pointer.
notes_text: This is a starred/important concept. The two-case pattern (empty vs non-empty) applies to virtually every linked list operation: push_back, push_front, pop_back, pop_front, find, print, destructor, etc. Forgetting to handle the empty case is one of the most common sources of segmentation faults in linked list code.

images.description: Two diagrams showing the empty case (head pointer containing 0x0) and the non-empty case (head at 0x148 pointing to a chain of three nodes with values 3, 9, and 2).

title: Building A Linked List (4) - Inserting a Second Item
summary: To insert a second item using push_back, we need to walk to the last element in the list and append the new item there.
main_text: To insert a second item, what would need to change in our current list? The push_back function handles the empty case with if(head == NULL){ ... } and the non-empty case in the else block where we need to walk to the last element. The code shows: void List::push_back(int v) { if(head == NULL){ ... } else { // Walk to the last element } }. After push_back(3) and push_back(9), head at 0x148 points to the node with val=3 whose next pointer (previously NULL) now needs to point to the new node with val=9.
notes_text: The key insight is that for push_back on a non-empty list, we cannot simply use the head pointer to add the new item. We must traverse the entire list to find the last element (the one whose next is NULL), then set that element's next pointer to the newly allocated item.

images.description: Diagram showing head at 0x148 pointing to node with val=3 and next=(NULL), with a new node containing val=9 that needs to be linked, illustrating the need to walk to the last element.

title: Building A Linked List (5) - Iterating to the Last Element
summary: For push_back on a non-empty list, we must iterate to the last element using the head pointer since that is our only entry point into the list.
main_text: To insert a second item, what would need to change in our current list? Answer: The last element in the list. When the list is NON-EMPTY with ONE or MANY elements already in the list, we must iterate to the last element in the list to insert our new Item. Given that we only have the head pointer, how do we step through the list? The code shows three push_back calls: mylist.push_back(3), mylist.push_back(9), mylist.push_back(2). The resulting list has head at 0x148 pointing to val=3 (next=0x1c0), then val=9 (next=0x0 NULL), then val=2 (next=0x0 NULL) as a separate node to be linked.
notes_text: This slide emphasizes that the only way to access elements in a singly linked list is through the head pointer and then following next pointers. There is no random access. To reach the last element, you must visit every element before it. This is fundamentally different from arrays where you can jump to any index.

images.description: Diagram showing a linked list with head at 0x148, nodes with values 3, 9, and 2 at addresses 0x148, 0x1c0, and 0x164, with the last node needing to be reached for push_back.

title: Building A Linked List (6) - Why Not Use Head to Traverse
summary: Do NOT use the head pointer to step through the list because moving head causes us to lose track of the beginning of the list permanently.
main_text: Given that we only have the head pointer, how do we step through the list? Would we even WANT TO use head to step through the list? No!!! The code shows a while loop: while( /* TBD */ ) { head = _____________; }. BEFORE: head at 0x148, pointing to nodes 3->9. AFTER (incorrectly using head to traverse): head moves to 0x1c0, now pointing to the second node (val=9). The first node (val=3 at 0x148) is now orphaned -- we have lost access to it. The head pointer has been overwritten and we can no longer find the start of the list.
notes_text: This is Common Linked List Mistake 1. If you use head = head->next to step through the list, you permanently lose the address of the first node. Since head is the only way to access the list, this effectively destroys part of the list. The solution is to use a temporary pointer variable instead.

images.description: Before and after diagrams showing how using head to traverse causes head to move from 0x148 to 0x1c0, losing access to the first node (val=3). Before shows head at 0x148, after shows head at 0x1c0 with the first node orphaned.

title: Common Linked List Mistake 1 - Losing the Head
summary: Changing head to traverse the list causes amnesia -- we forget where the list starts. Solution: do NOT change head, use a temp pointer instead.
main_text: If we change head we have no way to remember where the 1st item is. Once we take a step we have 'amnesia' and forget where we came from and can't retrace our steps. Lesson: Don't lose your head! Solution: Do NOT change head and use a temp pointer. BEFORE: head at 0x148, pointing to nodes with val=3 (next=0x1c0) and val=9 (next=NULL). AFTER using temp: head stays at 0x148 (unchanged), and a new Item* temp pointer at 0x148 is used to traverse. The temp pointer can be moved without affecting head.
notes_text: The lesson 'Don't lose your head' is a memorable mnemonic. The temp pointer is a local variable that copies the value of head, then can be safely advanced through the list using temp = temp->next. Head remains pointing to the first element throughout the traversal.

images.description: Before and after diagrams showing the correct approach: head stays at 0x148 while a separate temp pointer (also starting at 0x148) is used for traversal, preserving access to the start of the list.

title: Building a Linked List (7) - Using a Temp Pointer
summary: When the list is not empty, initialize a temp pointer to head and step through the list. Two key questions: what code takes a step, and when to stop.
main_text: When the list is NOT EMPTY use a temp pointer (initialized with head) and then stepping through the list to the last element. Questions: What code would we use to 'take a step'? When would we want to stop (and thus what condition would we use in our while loop)? The code shows: void List::push_back(int v) { if(head == NULL){ ... } else { // Iterate to last element Item* temp = head; while( /* when to stop? */ ) { temp = _____________ // take a step } } }. The diagram shows head at 0x148, temp also at 0x148, and three nodes with values 3, 9, 2 at addresses 0x148, 0x1c0, 0x164.
notes_text: The two key questions here are answered in the next slides: taking a step means temp = temp->next, and the stopping condition is when temp->next == NULL (meaning temp is at the last element). Using temp != NULL as the stop condition would go one step too far -- temp would be NULL and we couldn't modify the last node's next pointer.

images.description: Diagram showing head and temp both pointing to 0x148, with three linked nodes at 0x148 (val=3), 0x1c0 (val=9), and 0x164 (val=2), illustrating the starting position for traversal.

title: Common LL Task: Taking a Step
summary: To move from one item to the next in a linked list, use temp = temp->next. This advances the pointer to follow the next link.
main_text: What is the C++ code to take a step from one item to the next? Answer: temp = temp->next. Lesson: To move a pointer to the next item use: temp = temp->next. The code context shows the push_back function with Item* temp = head; and while loop with temp = temp->next as the step. BEFORE: temp at 0x148 pointing to node with val=3. AFTER: temp at 0x1c0 pointing to node with val=9. The head pointer remains at 0x148 unchanged.
notes_text: The expression temp = temp->next reads the next pointer from the current node and stores it in temp, effectively advancing temp to point to the next node. This is the fundamental operation for linked list traversal. Note that head is never modified during this process.

images.description: Before and after diagrams showing temp moving from 0x148 (pointing to val=3) to 0x1c0 (pointing to val=9) after executing temp = temp->next, while head stays at 0x148.

title: When Should We Stop Iterating
summary: Stop when temp->next is NULL (Option 1), not when temp is NULL (Option 2), because we need to modify the last element's next pointer to link the new node.
main_text: Option 1: When temp->next is NULL? Option 2: When temp is NULL? We need to modify the LAST element's next pointer, so we must stop when temp->next is NULL. If we stop when temp is NULL, we have gone one step past the last element and lost access to it. The code shows: while(temp->next != NULL) { temp = temp->next // take a step }. Option 1 stops temp at 0x1c0 (the last node with val=9, whose next is NULL). Option 2 would advance temp to 0x0 (NULL), which is one step too far and we can no longer access the last node.
notes_text: This distinction is critical. For push_back, we need to modify the last node's next pointer to point to the new node. If temp is NULL, we have no node to modify. By checking temp->next != NULL, we stop when temp IS the last node, allowing us to set temp->next = newNode. This is a common source of bugs for beginners.

images.description: Diagram showing two options for where temp stops. Option 1 has temp at 0x1c0 (pointing to the last node with val=9). Option 2 has temp at 0x0 (NULL), having gone past the end. Option 1 is correct.

title: Building a Linked List (8) - Complete Push Back Solution
summary: Complete push_back implementation for non-empty list: use temp to iterate to last element, allocate new node with new, set its fields, and link it via temp->next.
main_text: When the list is NOT EMPTY use a temp pointer (initialized with head) and then stepping through the list to the last element. Solution shown: void List::push_back(int v) { if(head == NULL){ ... } else { Item* temp = head; while(temp->next != NULL) { temp = temp->next // take a step } Item* newp = new Item; newp->val = v; newp->next = NULL; temp->next = newp; } }. After calling mylist.push_back(3), mylist.push_back(9), mylist.push_back(2): temp ends at 0x1c0 (node with val=9), newp is at 0x164. The node at 0x1c0 has its next changed from NULL to 0x164, linking the new node with val=2.
notes_text: This is the complete push_back solution. The steps are: (1) initialize temp = head, (2) walk temp to the last node using while(temp->next != NULL), (3) allocate a new Item on the heap, (4) set its val and next=NULL, (5) link it by setting temp->next = newp. The entire push_back operation is O(n) because we must traverse the entire list to find the end.

images.description: Diagram showing the final state after push_back(2): head at 0x148, temp at 0x1c0, newp at 0x164. Three nodes linked: 3->9->2->NULL. The temp pointer found the last node (val=9) and linked newp (val=2) to it.

title: Removing Items (e.g. the front) [1]
summary: Introduction to removal operations. Students are asked to determine what code is needed to remove the front item using pop_front.
main_text: Now let's look at removal. What code is necessary to remove the FRONT item? Modify the diagram below to show what we would WANT to happen. The code shows: void List::pop_front() { // What code goes here }. In main(): List mylist; mylist.push_back(3); mylist.push_back(9); mylist.push_back(2); mylist.pop_front();. The current state shows head at 0x148, nodes: 3 (0x148, next=0x1c0) -> 9 (0x1c0, next=0x164) -> 2 (0x164, next=NULL). The desired outcome is to remove the first node (val=3) and have head point to the second node (val=9).
notes_text: Removal from the front is simpler than from the back because we do not need to traverse the list. However, there are subtle issues with order of operations: we need to save the address of the first node before moving head, then delete the old first node. These issues are explored in the following slides.

images.description: Linked list diagram showing head at 0x148 pointing to three nodes with values 3, 9, 2. Students need to determine what the list should look like after removing the front item.

title: Removing Items (e.g. the front) [2] - Simply Updating Head
summary: Simply updating head to head->next skips the first node but causes a memory leak because the old first node is never freed.
main_text: Could we simply update head? Unfortunately, that causes a problem. The code shows: void List::pop_front() { // What code goes here head = head->next; }. After execution, head moves from 0x148 to 0x1c0, now pointing to the node with val=9. However, the node at 0x148 (val=3) is still allocated on the heap but is no longer accessible. This is a memory leak -- the old first node cannot be freed because we no longer have a pointer to it. The prohibition sign indicates this approach is wrong.
notes_text: Memory leaks occur when dynamically allocated memory is no longer reachable by any pointer. In this case, the node with val=3 still occupies heap memory but has no pointer referring to it. Over time, repeated memory leaks can consume all available memory. We need to delete the old node before or after updating head.

images.description: Diagram showing head moved to 0x1c0 after head = head->next, with the node at 0x148 (val=3) now orphaned and marked with a prohibition sign, indicating a memory leak.

title: Removing Items (e.g. the front) [3] - Delete Before Update Problem
summary: Deleting head first then updating head->next fails because after delete, head points to freed memory and accessing head->next is undefined behavior.
main_text: To avoid a memory leak, we CANNOT just change head. We need to free/delete the old first item! But what is wrong with the given code? The code shows: void List::pop_front() { delete head; head = head->next; }. The problem is that after delete head, the memory at 0x148 is freed. Then head = head->next tries to access the next pointer of the deleted node, which is undefined behavior -- the memory has been returned to the system. The diagram shows head being crossed out at 0x148, with the node at 0x148 being deleted but then trying to read its next field.
notes_text: This is the chicken-and-egg problem: we need head->next to know where the second item is, but we also need to delete the first item to avoid a leak. We cannot do both with just the head pointer -- we need a temporary pointer to save the address of the first item (or the second item) before performing the delete.

images.description: Diagram showing the problem of deleting head first: the node at 0x148 is freed (marked with prohibition sign), then head = head->next tries to access freed memory, which is invalid.

title: Removing Items (e.g. the front) [4] - Correct Solution with Temp Pointer
summary: Correct pop_front: save head in a temp pointer, update head to temp->next, then delete temp. This avoids both memory leaks and use-after-free.
main_text: To avoid the chicken vs. egg problem about deleting the first item vs. using it to get the second item's address, let's introduce a temp pointer. Three steps: 1. Introduce a temp pointer that is a copy of head. 2. Get the next pointer from the first item to update head. 3. Delete the old first item. The correct code: void List::pop_front() { Item* temp = head; head = temp->next; delete temp; }. Step 1: temp = head (both point to 0x148). Step 2: head = temp->next (head moves to 0x1c0). Step 3: delete temp (frees the node at 0x148). The diagram shows numbered steps with temp at 0x148, head moving to 0x1c0, and the old first node being deleted.
notes_text: This is the correct pattern for removing the front item. The temp pointer preserves access to the node being removed, allowing us to both update head and free the memory. This pattern (save, redirect, delete) is used frequently in linked list operations. Note that this does not handle the edge case of an empty list -- in production code you would check if head is NULL first.

images.description: Numbered step diagram showing: (1) temp copies head at 0x148, (2) head updates to 0x1c0 via temp->next, (3) delete temp frees the node at 0x148. Prohibition signs mark the deleted node.

title: Final Result After Remove
summary: After executing pop_front, the list correctly has head pointing to the second node (val=9) with the first node (val=3) properly deleted.
main_text: After execution of pop_front(): The correct code is: Item* temp = head; head = temp->next; delete temp;. The final state shows head at 0x1c0 pointing to the node with val=9 (next=0x164), which points to val=2 (next=NULL). The node that previously held val=3 at 0x148 has been properly freed. In main(): List mylist; mylist.push_back(3); mylist.push_back(9); mylist.push_back(2); mylist.pop_front();
notes_text: The final list after pop_front contains only two elements: 9 and 2. The memory for the removed node (val=3) has been properly returned to the heap via delete. No memory leak occurs and no undefined behavior is triggered because we used the temp pointer pattern.

images.description: Final linked list state showing head at 0x1c0 pointing to node with val=9 (next=0x164), then node with val=2 (next=NULL). The deleted node at 0x148 is no longer shown.

title: Recall: Destructors
summary: A destructor (~ClassName) is called automatically when an object goes out of scope or is deleted. Data members are cleaned up automatically but pointed-to resources are not.
main_text: Destructor (dtor for short) is a function of the same name as class itself with a ~ in front (e.g. ~Deck()). Called automatically when object goes out of scope (i.e. when it is deallocated by 'delete' or when scope completes). Returns nothing. Important: Data members of an object are cleaned up / destroyed automatically by the destructor (without you adding any code). Note: The Deck class did not require a destructor. Example shows class Deck with constructor Deck(), destructor ~Deck(), private members int cards[52] and int top_index. The Deck destructor body is empty: { /* not needed for this class */ }. In main, Deck d is created (Deck() called), and ~Deck() is called automatically at return 0.
notes_text: This review of destructors sets up the need for a List destructor. The Deck class only has stack-allocated members (an array and an int), so they are automatically cleaned up. But the List class has a head pointer to heap-allocated nodes -- those nodes will NOT be automatically freed, causing memory leaks unless the destructor explicitly deletes them.

images.description: Code files deck.h, deck.cpp, and cardgame.cpp showing the Deck class definition, empty destructor implementation, and main function where Deck constructor and destructor are called automatically.

title: Need for Destructor in Linked List
summary: The List destructor must explicitly delete all heap-allocated nodes because the automatic cleanup only destroys the head pointer itself, not the nodes it points to.
main_text: Important: Data members of an object are cleaned up / destroyed automatically by the destructor (without you adding any code). Implication: Your destructor does NOT need to worry about deallocation or cleaning up your data members. Your destructor NEEDS to clean up things that your data members POINT TO or REFERENCE that won't be cleaned up if your data member(s) die. So, we'd need to deallocate each item remaining in the list. The List destructor must walk the list and delete each Item. Code shows: List::~List() { // Do we need code to clean up what our members refer to? }. After pop_front, the remaining list has head at 0x1c0 pointing to val=9 (next=0x164) and val=2 (next=NULL). When ~List() is called, head (the pointer variable) is automatically destroyed, but the nodes it points to remain on the heap -- a memory leak without explicit cleanup.
notes_text: The destructor must iterate through the list and delete each node, similar to calling pop_front repeatedly until the list is empty. A common implementation uses a while loop: while(head != NULL) { Item* temp = head; head = head->next; delete temp; }. This ensures all heap memory is reclaimed.

images.description: Diagram showing head pointer at 0x1c0 with a prohibition sign, pointing to two heap-allocated nodes (val=9 and val=2). When head is destroyed, the nodes remain as leaked memory.

title: Destructors: Another Example - Memory Leak Without Destructor
summary: When a LinkedList object on the stack goes out of scope without a destructor, its head pointer is destroyed but heap-allocated nodes remain, causing a memory leak.
main_text: The LinkedList object is allocated as a static/local variable, but each element is allocated on the heap. When y goes out of scope only the data members are deallocated. You may have a memory leak. The struct Item has int val and Item* next. The class LinkedList has void push_back(int v) and private Item* head. In doTask(), LinkedList y is created, then y.push_back(3) and y.push_back(5) are called. When doTask returns, the stack frame for doTask is destroyed, including the LinkedList object y and its head pointer. But the two heap-allocated nodes (val=3 at 0x93c and val=5 at 0x748) remain in memory with no pointer to them. The label 'MEMORY LEAK: When y is deallocated we have no pointer to the data' is shown.
notes_text: This example concretely shows the stack vs heap distinction. The LinkedList object y lives on the stack within doTask's stack frame. When doTask returns, y's stack memory (including the head pointer) is reclaimed. But the Items were allocated with 'new' on the heap, and without a destructor to delete them, they leak.

images.description: Memory diagram showing stack area with doTask and main frames, and heap area with two nodes (val=3, val=5). When doTask's frame is popped, the head pointer in y is destroyed but heap nodes persist as leaked memory.

title: Destructors: Another Example - Solution with Destructor
summary: An appropriate destructor will solve the memory leak problem by walking the list and deleting each node before the object is destroyed.
main_text: The LinkedList object is allocated as a static/local variable, but each element is allocated on the heap. When y goes out of scope only the data members are deallocated. You may have a memory leak. An Appropriate Destructor Will Help Solve This. The same struct Item and class LinkedList are shown. In main, doTask() is called, which creates LinkedList y, calls y.push_back(3) and y.push_back(5). The stack/heap diagram shows the same layout but now with the message 'An Appropriate Destructor Will Help Solve This' highlighted. When doTask returns, the destructor ~LinkedList() is called automatically before y's memory is reclaimed, giving it a chance to delete all heap-allocated nodes.
notes_text: The destructor is the C++ mechanism for deterministic cleanup. It is called automatically at the right time (when the object goes out of scope or is deleted), making it the ideal place to free heap-allocated resources. This is the RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization) pattern: the constructor acquires resources and the destructor releases them.

images.description: Same stack/heap diagram as slide 31, but with a prominent label 'An Appropriate Destructor Will Help Solve This' indicating that adding a destructor prevents the memory leak.
labels: An Appropriate Destructor Will Help Solve This

title: Comparing Performance - Arrays vs Linked Lists (Exercise)
summary: Exercise comparing Big-O complexity for common operations on arrays vs linked lists: element access, adding to tail, and adding to front.
main_text: Arrays: Go to element at index i: O(__). Add something to the tail (assume you have a tail index): O(__). Adding something to the front of the list after there are already n elements: O(__). Linked Lists: Go to element at index i: O(__). Add something to the tail (assume you have only head pointer and n elements in the list): O(__). Adding something to the front of the list after there are already n elements: O(__). The blanks are left for students to fill in as an exercise.
notes_text: The answers are provided on slide 44. For arrays: O(1) for index access, O(1) for tail add with tail index, O(n) for front add (must shift all elements). For linked lists: O(i) or O(n) for index access (must traverse), O(n) for tail add with only head (must traverse), O(1) for front add (just update head). This comparison highlights the complementary strengths of each data structure.

title: Odds and Ends Section Divider
summary: Section divider slide marking the beginning of the Odds and Ends section covering additional linked list topics and common mistakes.
main_text: ODDS AND ENDS. This section covers additional topics, common mistakes, and useful patterns for working with linked lists.
notes_text: This section revisits common mistakes and tasks as a review and reference, reinforcing the key lessons from the main lecture content.

title: Common Linked List Mistake 1 (Repeated) - Don't Lose Your Head
summary: Review: changing head to traverse loses the list's starting address. Always use a temp pointer to preserve head.
main_text: If we change head we have no way to remember where the 1st item is. Once we take a step we have 'amnesia' and forget where we came from and can't retrace our steps. Lesson: Don't lose your head! Solution: Do NOT change head and use a temp pointer. The code shows push_back with a while loop where head = _____________ would incorrectly modify head. BEFORE: head at 0x148, nodes 3->9. AFTER (correct): head stays at 0x148, temp pointer at 0x148 is used instead for traversal. Head remains unchanged while temp advances through the list.
notes_text: This is a repeated slide from the main content (same as slide 19), included in the Odds and Ends section for review and reference. The key takeaway remains: never modify head during traversal operations.

images.description: Before and after diagrams showing head preserved at 0x148 while temp pointer is used for traversal, with nodes containing values 3 and 9.

title: Common Linked Task/Mistake 2 - Head is Not an Item
summary: Head is just a pointer, not an Item struct. Use head (not head->next) to get a pointer to the first item. Many students mistakenly think head->next points to the first item.
main_text: What code will give us a pointer to the beginning item in the list? Mistake: Many students think head->next is how you get a pointer to the first item: Item* temp = head->next; (WRONG). Just use head to get the pointer to the beginning item. head is special. It is NOT an actual ITEM struct. head is just a pointer that points to the beginning (data-filled) item struct. head->next actually points to the 2nd item, not the 1st because head already points to the 1st item. Lesson: To get a pointer to the FIRST item, just use head. A train analogy is shown: the engine represents head (not a data car), and each train car represents an Item. Students mistakenly think head is an Item with val and next fields, or that head->next gives the first item.
notes_text: This mistake stems from confusing the head pointer with a node. Head is an Item* (a pointer TO an Item), not an Item itself. It does not have val or next fields. Only the Items (nodes) have those fields. Item* temp = head correctly gives a pointer to the first node. Item* temp = head->next gives a pointer to the SECOND node.

images.description: Train analogy showing engine (head) pulling data cars (Items). Diagrams show the correct understanding (head points to first Item) vs mistakes (thinking head->next is the first item, or thinking head itself is an Item with val/next fields).
labels: Mistake: Thinking head->next is a pointer to the first Item
Mistake: Students think head is an Item

title: Common Linked Task/Mistake 3 - Unnecessary Allocation
summary: Do not use 'new' when creating a temporary pointer for traversal. Just declare the pointer and assign it. Using new allocates an unnecessary Item that causes a memory leak.
main_text: Common errors we see is that to create a temporary pointer students also dynamically allocate an item and then immediately point it at something else causing a memory leak. Item* temp = new Item; then temp = head; or temp = head->next; (WRONG -- the allocated Item is leaked). You may declare pointers without having to allocate anything: Item* temp; (uninitialized), Item* temp = NULL; (initialized to null), Item* temp = head; (initialized to head's value). Lesson: Only use 'new' when you really want a new Item to come alive (i.e. in functions that are supposed to add an Item to the list). The diagram shows: Item* temp=NULL stores 0x00, Item* temp=head stores 0x148, Item* temp stores ??? (uninitialized). The mistake diagram shows temp allocated at 0x240 pointing to a new Item, then immediately overwritten to point to head, leaving the allocated Item leaked.
notes_text: This is a very common beginner mistake. Students associate pointer declaration with allocation, but pointers are just variables that hold addresses. Declaring Item* temp = head simply copies head's address into temp -- no new memory is allocated. Using 'new' creates a real Item on the heap, and if you immediately overwrite the pointer, that Item becomes unreachable (leaked).

images.description: Diagram showing the mistake of allocating with new Item then overwriting with head, causing a memory leak at address 0x240. Also shows correct pointer declarations without allocation: temp=NULL (0x00), temp=head (0x148), temp uninitialized (???).
labels: Mistake: Allocating an item when you declare a temporary pointer

title: Other Functions - Print, Find, Remove by Value
summary: Overview of additional linked list operations: printing all items, finding an item by value, and removing an item by value (which requires updating the previous node's next pointer).
main_text: Write a function to print all items in list: Copy head to a temp pointer then use it to iterate over the items until the next pointer is NULL. Print each item as you iterate. Find if an item in the list (return address of struct if present or NULL): Copy head to a temp pointer then use it to iterate over the items until you find an item with the desired value or until next pointer is NULL. Remove item with given value (i.e. find and remove): If found, need to change the next link of the previous item to point at the item after the item found. Example shows removing VAL=9 from list: head at 0x148, nodes 3 (next=0x168) -> 9 (next=0x168) -> 2 (next=NULL). To remove 9, the node with val=3 has its next changed from 0x1c0 to 0x168, bypassing the node with val=9.
notes_text: For remove-by-value, you need to track the previous node so you can update its next pointer. This can be done with two pointers (prev and curr) or by looking ahead (checking temp->next->val). The edge case where the item to remove is the first item (head) must be handled separately since there is no previous node -- you update head directly.

images.description: Diagram showing removal of node with val=9: the node with val=3 has its next pointer changed to skip over val=9 and point directly to val=2, with the removed node's links crossed out.

title: Common Linked List Mistake 1 Solution - Use Temp Pointer
summary: Solution: if we change head we lose access to the first item. Use a temp pointer initialized to head for traversal instead of modifying head directly.
main_text: If we change head we have no way to remember where the 1st item is. Once we take a step we have 'amnesia' and forget where we came from and can't retrace our steps. Lesson: Don't lose your head! Solution: Do NOT change head and use a temp pointer. The push_back code shows the else branch with a while loop for iterating to the last element. Using head = _____________ to step would destroy the list. BEFORE: head at 0x148. AFTER (correct solution): head remains at 0x148, temp at 0x148 is used for traversal. Two linked nodes shown: val=3 (next=0x1c0) and val=9 (next=NULL).
notes_text: This is the solution version of Common Mistake 1, confirming the temp pointer approach. The pattern Item* temp = head; while(...) { temp = temp->next; } is the standard traversal idiom for singly linked lists.

images.description: Before and after diagrams confirming the solution: head stays at 0x148 while temp pointer handles traversal through nodes with values 3 and 9.

title: Common Mistake 2 Solution - Use Head for First Item
summary: Solution: head is just a pointer, not an Item. To get a pointer to the first item, use head directly. head->next points to the second item, not the first.
main_text: What code will give us a pointer to the beginning item in the list? Mistake: Many students think head->next is how you get a pointer to the first item: Item* temp = head->next; (WRONG). Just use head to get the pointer to the beginning item. head is special. It is NOT an actual ITEM struct. head is just a pointer that points to the beginning (data-filled) item struct. head->next actually points to the 2nd item, not the 1st because head already points to the 1st item. Lesson: To get a pointer to the FIRST item, just use head. Train analogy: Engine = head, Each car = Item. Mistake diagrams show: (1) Thinking head->next is a pointer to the first Item (temp = head->next gives 0x1c0, the second node). (2) Students thinking head is an Item with a question mark for val.
notes_text: This solution slide confirms that Item* temp = head is the correct way to get a pointer to the first item. The train analogy is helpful: the engine (head) pulls the first car (first Item), so the engine IS the reference to the first car. You don't need to go to the next car to find the first one.

images.description: Train analogy and diagrams showing correct usage (head points to first item) vs common mistakes (thinking head->next gives the first item, or thinking head is an Item struct).
labels: Mistake: Thinking head->next is a pointer to the first Item
Mistake: Students think head is an Item

title: Common Mistake 3 Solution - Don't Allocate for Temp Pointers
summary: Solution: only use new when adding a node to the list. Declaring a temporary pointer requires no allocation -- just assign it to head or NULL.
main_text: Common errors we see is when creating a temporary pointer, students also dynamically allocate an item and then immediately point it at something else causing a memory leak. Item* temp = new Item; then temp = head; or temp = head->next; (the new Item is leaked). You may declare pointers without having to allocate anything: Item* temp; (uninitialized), Item* temp = NULL; (safe default), Item* temp = head; (pointing to first node). Lesson: Only use 'new' when you really want a new Item to come alive (i.e. in functions that are supposed to add an Item to the list). Correct: Item* temp=NULL stores 0x00, Item* temp=head stores 0x148, Item* temp stores ??? (uninitialized, assign with temp = head to get 0x148).
notes_text: The rule is simple: use 'new' only in push_back, push_front, or insert operations where you actually want to create a new node. For traversal, searching, or removal operations, just declare a pointer variable and point it at an existing node. No allocation needed.

images.description: Diagram showing correct pointer declarations without allocation and the mistake of allocating then overwriting, with before/after traversal states.
labels: Mistake: Allocating an item when you declare a temporary pointer

title: Common Task 1 Solution - Taking a Step
summary: Solution: to move a pointer to the next item in a linked list, use temp = temp->next. This follows the next pointer to advance to the subsequent node.
main_text: What is the C++ code to take a step from one item to the next? Answer: temp = temp->next. Lesson: To move a pointer to the next item use: ptr = ptr->next. The diagram shows head at 0x148, two nodes: val=3 (next=0x1c0) and val=9 (next=0x0 NULL). Before taking step: temp = 0x148 (pointing to first node). After taking step: temp = 0x1c0 (pointing to second node). The operation temp = temp->next reads the next field of the current node (0x1c0) and stores it in temp, advancing the pointer.
notes_text: This is the fundamental linked list traversal operation. The expression temp->next accesses the next pointer stored in the node that temp currently points to. Assigning this value back to temp makes temp point to the next node. This is equivalent to incrementing an array index (i++) but for linked structures.

images.description: Diagram showing temp pointer advancing from 0x148 to 0x1c0 after executing temp = temp->next, with two linked nodes (val=3 and val=9) and before/after labels.

title: Comparing Performance - Arrays vs Linked Lists (Answers)
summary: Performance answers: Arrays have O(1) access and tail add, O(n) front add. Linked lists have O(i) access, O(n) tail add (head only), O(1) front add.
main_text: Arrays: Go to element at index i: O(1). Add something to the tail (assume you have a tail index): O(1). Adding something to the front of the list after there are already n elements: O(n). Linked Lists: Go to element at index i: O(i). Add something to the tail (assume you have only head pointer and n elements in the list): O(n). Adding something to the front of the list after there are already n elements: O(1). Arrays excel at random access (O(1)) and tail operations with a tail index. Linked lists excel at front insertion/deletion (O(1)) and dynamic resizing. Arrays struggle with front insertion (O(n) shifts required). Linked lists struggle with random access (O(i) traversal) and tail operations without a tail pointer (O(n) traversal).
notes_text: This comparison is fundamental to choosing the right data structure. If your use case involves frequent random access, use an array. If your use case involves frequent insertions/deletions at the front, use a linked list. A tail pointer can improve linked list tail operations to O(1). The O(i) notation for linked list access emphasizes that accessing the first element is O(1) but accessing the last is O(n).
